title: The Arabian Nights (Shéherazade)
subtitle: Tell to survive
subject: mythologie
description: Scheherazade survives 1001 nights by telling stories. A collection born between Persia, Baghdad and Egypt, which has become a world myth.

hero.hook: Every night, a woman tells a story so as not to die at dawn.

blocks.text: The **Arabian Nights** (*Alf Layla wa-Layla*) is not a book by a single author. It's a palimpsest: centuries of oral and written tales, Indian, Persian, Arab, Egyptian.

In the center, a dizzying idea: a woman, **Scheherazade**, transforms the story into a shield. As long as she speaks, the king who wanted to kill her must wait. This is how speech becomes a weapon of survival.

sections.title: An architecture of paper: the genesis of a world-text

blocks.text: The core comes from a Persian source, the [[Hazār Afsāna]] (“A Thousand Tales”), themselves nourished by Indian traditions. In Baghdad, under the [[Abbasids]] caliphs (8th-13th centuries), the collection became Arabized: urban legends, court anecdotes, sometimes satirical tone.

blocks.caption: Manuscript of the Thousand and One Nights: a world-text in formation.

blocks.text: “A thousand and one” does not mean an exact count. In Arabic, this number suggests abundance, almost infinity. Some scribes even saw it as a talisman against the evil eye.

In Egypt, at the time of , new cycles were added. Surprise for the West: **Aladdin** and **Ali Baba** are missing from medieval Arabic manuscripts. These are “orphan tales”, entered later via Europe. [[Mamluks]]

sections.title: The Hegemony of Scheherazade: narration as a shield

blocks.text: King **Shahryar**, betrayed by his first wife, marries a young woman every evening and has her killed at dawn. **Scheherazade**, daughter of the vizier, offers herself. She tells… and stops at the most tense moment.

blocks.caption: Scheherazade facing Shahryar: narration as a shield.

blocks.text: She piles up s: one character tells another, who tells a third. The king, captive to the desire to hear what happens next, postpones the execution. After **A Thousand and One Nights**, listening changed Shahryar: he found empathy again. Scheherazade didn't just entertain. She fixed a tyrant. [[nested stories (frame narrative)]]

sections.title: The shift towards the West and the invention of a myth

blocks.text: Between **1704** and **1717**, the French orientalist **Antoine Galland** publishes his translation. He adapts the text to the taste of the court of **Louis XIV** and adds tales heard from , a passing Syrian. Aladdin thus enters the corpus. [[Hanna Diyab]]

blocks.caption: Galland opens the Nights to 18th century Europe.

blocks.text: Young people sometimes woke Galland up at night by shouting under his window: “Mr. Galland, if you can’t sleep, tell us one of your stories!” »

Success invents a [[European Orientalism]]: flying carpets, genies, caliphs in disguise. Fantasy vision, often reductive, but of immense influence, from **Proust** to **Borges**, who saw in these narrative loops the very image of literary infinity.

sections.title: Modernity and philosophical scope of the story

blocks.text: Why tell? The Nights answer: to keep death at bay. As long as Scheherazade's voice resonates, the fatal dawn is suspended. Fiction gives form to chaos.
This mechanism still nourishes our series: the [[cliffhanger]], this cut on the edge of the precipice, is the direct heir of the narrator. A book open to infinity, which refuses to close.
**Scheherazade** survives **1001** nights thanks to embedded stories: she invents suspense as a survival tool, and transforms speech into political power.
